title: Physical change
body: A change in a substance's properties but not its composition, such as a phase change or the formation or separation of a mixture.

title: Chemical change
body: A change in which substances are transformed into new substances, typically with different compositions.

title: Possible evidence of a chemical change
body: Observations that may indicate a chemical change has occurred.
caution: These are only possible evidence, not proof; a physical change can also produce some of them.

title: Balanced equations conserve atoms and charge
body: Any equation for a chemical change must have equal numbers of atoms of every element on both sides, which shows that mass and charge are conserved.

title: Three symbolic forms of a reaction equation
body: Differing symbolic forms of the same reaction; the context determines which one to use.

items.label: Balanced molecular equation
items.meaning: Symbolic form for representing a reaction

items.label: Complete ionic equation
items.meaning: Symbolic form for representing a reaction

items.label: Net ionic equation
items.meaning: Symbolic form for representing a reaction

title: Physical changes can be written as balanced equations too
body: Physical as well as chemical processes can be represented symbolically by balanced equations.

title: Particulate representation of a balanced equation
body: A balanced equation in any form can be translated into a consistent particulate model.

items.label: Atom conservation
items.meaning: Equal numbers of atoms of each element before and after

title: Classifying processes by bonds versus intermolecular interactions
body: Processes that break or form chemical bonds are typically chemical, and processes involving only changes in intermolecular interactions, such as phase changes, are typically physical.
caution: Dissolving a salt in water can be argued as either physical or chemical, since ionic bonds break and ion-dipole interactions form; support whichever claim you make with that evidence.

title: Coefficients give mole ratios
body: Coefficients of a balanced equation give the proportions of the amounts (in moles) of the substances involved, and these are used with the mole concept to find product amounts from reactant amounts or the reverse.
caution: Compare moles, not masses, when determining a limiting reactant, and convert to mass with molar mass when a mass is asked for.

title: Molarity
body: M = \frac{n_{\text{solute}}}{V_{\text{solution}}}

title: Ideal gas law
body: PV = nRT
ced_evidence: 4.5.A.3 (stoichiometry combined with the ideal gas law)

title: Titrant and analyte
body: The titrant is the solution of known concentration that reacts specifically and quantitatively with the analyte, the species whose amount is being determined.

title: Equivalence point
body: The point in a titration at which the analyte is totally consumed by the reacting species in the titrant.

title: Endpoint
body: The observable event, such as a color change, that indicates the equivalence point has been reached.
caution: The endpoint is the observed signal; the equivalence point is the stoichiometric condition.

title: Three reaction types and what defines them
body: Reactions are identified as acid-base, redox, or precipitation by what is transferred or formed.

items.label: Acid-base
items.meaning: Transfer of one or more protons (H+) between species

items.label: Oxidation-reduction
items.meaning: Transfer of one or more electrons, shown by changes in oxidation numbers

items.label: Precipitation
items.meaning: Mixing aqueous ions to produce an insoluble or sparingly soluble ionic compound

caution: When asked to justify a reaction type, cite the equation evidence (proton transfer, oxidation-number change, or solid product formed).

title: Direction of electron transfer in redox
body: Electrons are transferred from the species that is oxidized to the species that is reduced, and oxidation numbers assigned to each atom identify which species is which.

hooks.when_to_use: When deciding which species is oxidized and which is reduced from oxidation-number changes.

title: Combustion
body: An important subclass of redox reactions in which a species reacts with oxygen gas; complete combustion of a hydrocarbon produces carbon dioxide and water.

title: Salts always soluble in water
body: The only solubility facts required by the CED: all salts of these ions are soluble.

title: Brønsted-Lowry acid and base
body: A Brønsted-Lowry acid is a proton donor and a Brønsted-Lowry base is a proton acceptor.

title: Conjugate acid-base pair
body: When an acid or base ionizes in water, the species related by the transfer of a proton form conjugate acid-base pairs whose relative strengths can be compared.

title: Water as proton donor and acceptor
body: In aqueous solutions, water can both accept protons from and donate protons to dissolved species, so it plays an important role in many acid-base reactions.

title: Building a balanced redox equation from half-reactions
body: Write the oxidation and reduction half-reactions with electrons shown (as products in the oxidation half-reaction), then combine them so the electrons cancel and atoms and charge are balanced.
caution: Omitting electrons or writing the reduction direction for the species that is oxidized (for example, at the anode) loses the point.
